steps.label: KP02 Knowing only the direction, how far to step
Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7
steps.speakerNotes: Training minimizes the loss over the parameters; each step needs an update. For small displacements the change in loss can be estimated to first order.

steps.label: Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The first-order estimate is the gradient transposed times the displacement.

steps.label: Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Choosing the displacement as minus the learning rate times the gradient, the change is about minus the learning rate times the squared gradient length.

steps.label: Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: A square is never negative, so the change is never positive: along the negative gradient the loss falls under the approximation.

steps.label: Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Written as an update this is gradient descent.

steps.label: Walk along the negative gradient · 1/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: The learning rate only scales; the distance is the learning rate times the gradient length. It is a local estimate that can fail for large steps, so we check.

steps.label: One complete step · 2/7
steps.speakerNotes: Use a quadratic loss as the main example. The minimum is at 0.4 with loss 0.2. Starting at w0 equal 2: derivative 16, loss 13.

steps.label: One complete step · 2/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With learning rate 0.05 the new parameter is 1.2 and the loss 3.4, a real decrease.

steps.label: One complete step · 2/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The gradient is positive, so the parameter moves left: the right direction.

steps.label: One complete step · 2/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Checking the sign is not enough; verify direction, step and the actual loss after the update.

steps.label: Late slowdown · 3/7
steps.speakerNotes: Keep updating with 0.05: the parameters are 2, 1.2, 0.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.45 and the losses 13, 3.4, 1, 0.4, 0.25, 0.2125.

steps.label: Late slowdown · 3/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Simplified the update is 0.5 times w plus 0.2, and the distance to the minimum halves each step.

steps.label: Late slowdown · 3/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Nearer the minimum the gradient is smaller and so are the steps, so late descent is slow.

steps.label: Late slowdown · 3/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: nearer the minimum the gradient is smaller, so steps shrink and late progress slows with a fixed learning rate the steps shrink by themselves

steps.label: Three fates · 4/7
steps.speakerNotes: For the same function the error is multiplied each step by 1 minus 10 times the learning rate. The start error is 1.6.

steps.label: Three fates · 4/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 0.02: factor 0.8, safe but slow.

steps.label: Three fates · 4/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 0.10: factor 0, straight to the minimum in one step.

steps.label: Three fates · 4/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 0.25: factor minus 1.5, overshooting the valley each time and running away, the bouncing ball.

steps.label: Three fates · 4/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: The start gap is 12.8; at 0.25 it becomes 28.8, larger than the start.

steps.label: The bouncing ball · 5/7
steps.speakerNotes: A simpler function w squared with start 4. Learning rate 0.1: the first step is 3.2, loss 10.24 below 16, shrinking.

steps.label: The bouncing ball · 5/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 1: 4, minus 4, 4, minus 4, bouncing between the sides with the loss stuck at 16.

steps.label: The bouncing ball · 5/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Learning rate 1.1: the first step is minus 4.8 with loss 23.04; the second 5.76 with loss 33.18: divergence.

steps.label: The bouncing ball · 5/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: \eta=1.1: diverges w_1=-4.8,\ f=23.04 w_2=5.76,\ f=33.18 overshooting the valley is not a decrease: at \eta=1 the loss never changes

steps.label: A safe step size · 6/7
steps.speakerNotes: Can we compute a safe learning rate in advance? Yes, if we know how curved the loss is. L-smooth means the gradient changes at a bounded rate; L is a property of the function.

steps.label: A safe step size · 6/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: This gives the descent lemma. The bracket must be positive for guaranteed descent, so the learning rate is below 2 over L; with 1 over L each step decreases at least a half over L times the squared gradient.

steps.label: A safe step size · 6/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In the main example the second derivative is 10, so L is 10. Learning rate 0.1 reaches the minimum in one step; 0.02 shrinks slowly; 0.25 exceeds 0.2 and diverges.

steps.label: A safe step size · 6/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Beware over-reading: 1 over L is a safe choice, not the only or largest step; strict decrease requires a nonzero gradient; in practice L of a deep network is hard to compute usefully, so we tune a fixed learning rate.

steps.label: A safe step size · 6/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: \eta=1/L is a safe choice, not the only or largest step; strict decrease also needs a nonzero gradient all three match the previous page: 0.1 one step, 0.02 slow, 0.25 diverges

steps.label: Convex vs non-convex · 7/7
steps.speakerNotes: A convex loss has no worse local minima. A non-convex loss can have many basins and saddle points.

steps.label: Convex vs non-convex · 7/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: For convex, smooth losses with a suitable step the loss can approach the global minimum; non-convex typically guarantees at most a gradient approaching zero.

steps.label: Convex vs non-convex · 7/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The start affects speed and path when convex, but can lead to different basins when non-convex.

steps.label: Convex vs non-convex · 7/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Oscillation on a non-convex loss is neither success nor failure; separate parameter oscillation, full-data loss and batch loss.

steps.label: Convex vs non-convex · 7/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: back-and-forth on a non-convex loss is neither success nor failure; a downward trend is not proof of convergence a deep network's loss is non-convex: many basins and saddle points
